newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pope honours controversial king in France.
newsitem.headline: Pope honours controversial king in France.

text.p: Pope John Paul honoured a long-dead king on the last day of a visit to France on Sunday, ignoring opponents who said the ceremony ran counter to the secular ideals of the 1789 Revolution.

The Pontiff landed at an airbase near Reims, eastern France, to give a mass to celebrate the 1,500th anniversary of the baptism of Clovis, the first king in western Europe to convert to Roman Catholicism.

Thousands of the faithful gathered for the Pope's biggest mass, camped out in chilly, misty weather to get a good view of the 76-year-old Pope, who flew in from Tours in western France. He walked unaided from the plane.
Police said 180,000 people had come to the mass, 30,000 more than had been expected.

Later in Paris, anti-papal demonstrators were due to hold the main protest rally of the Pontiff's four-day stay to denounce his conservative moral teachings and blast the Clovis celebrations as violating laws separating Church and State.

The Pontiff, looking relatively robust despite his gruelling schedule, was expected to seek to appease opponents by avoiding a traditional Catholic view that the conversion of Clovis marked the birth of France.
French Church leaders said he would use a sermon to stress the importance of baptism to modern Catholics.

Clovis was a central figure in French history before the 1789 Revolution cut short the monarchy -- the 16 kings named Louis were using a version of Clovis's name, and French monarchs were crowned in Reims in his honour.

In Paris, 70 anti-papal groups were staging a rally to accuse the Church, President Jacques Chirac and the political far right of trying to use Clovis, who they say was a brutal Dark Ages warlord, to revive belief that France is rightfully Catholic.

Clovis, born in what is now Belgium and who ruled an area stretching from eastern France to Germany, was baptised in Reims around 496. He extended his kingdom in battles against tribes like the Visigoths to cover most of France.

Opposition groups, including anarchists, Greens, Freemasons and police trade unions, will instead celebrate the traditions of the Revolution. The first French republic was proclaimed on September 22, 1792.

The umbrella alliance will also denounce the Pope's conservative teachings and oppostion to birth control, abortion and homosexuality. "For the separation of Church and State, against the return of moral order," their posters proclaim.

The Pontiff, on a visit that has taken him to Tours, Brittany and Vendee, has so far played down his controversial moral views -- which few French people follow -- and has stressed solidarity with the poor and the suffering.

The Pope upset France's other religious groups, mainly Moslems, Jews and Protestants, on his first visit in 1980 when he spoke of France's 1,500-year history as a nation. "France, eldest daughter of the Church, what have you done with the promises of your baptism?" he asked.

In Reims, the Pope was also scheduled meet France's bishops on Sunday, including "Red Cleric" Jacques Gaillot, sacked last year by the Vatican for his liberal views such as favouring condoms to prevent the spread of AIDS.
The Pontiff was to later visit Reims cathedral, almost wrecked during World War One, where Catholics say Clovis was baptised and where French monarchs were crowned.
After brief talks with Prime Minister Alain Juppe, he was to fly home in the early evening, ending his last trip abroad before an operation next month to remove his appendix.
